result: High-income countries, including Italy, are experiencing measles reemergence. Italy experienced a major outbreak in 2017 with 5098 cases (4042 laboratory-confirmed), four deaths, with 70% of cases in adults over 20 years (median age 27), suggesting adult transmission plays a significant role.
evaluation: Claims C1, C8-C13 are well-supported by citations to official health reports (Italian National Institute of Health, ECDC, WHO). The age distribution data and outbreak statistics are documented in authoritative sources, providing strong evidence for measles reemergence driven by adult susceptibility.

result: Significant immunity gaps exist in Italian adults aged 15-45 years, resulting from historical suboptimal vaccination coverage (below 80% until 2003, peaking at 91% in 2010—below the 95% elimination threshold) and absence of major epidemics allowing individuals to escape both vaccination and natural infection. Recent years show declining coverage possibly due to vaccine hesitancy.
evaluation: Claims C14-C25 are supported by multiple citations to serological studies (Rota et al. 2008), modeling studies (Merler and Ajelli 2014, Trentini et al. 2017), and historical vaccination data. The 95% threshold claim is appropriately cited to Anderson and May 1991, a foundational reference in infectious disease epidemiology.

result: In July 2017, Italy introduced mandatory vaccination at school entry (regulation 119/2017) for children under 16 years, with enforcement mechanisms including kindergarten exclusion and financial penalties. While this policy can increase childhood vaccination and catch up school-age children, it will not address existing immunity gaps in adults, and high childhood coverage alone may be insufficient for measles elimination.
evaluation: Claims C2, C26-C33 accurately describe Italian policy and are supported by appropriate citations (Signorelli et al. 2018, D'Ancona et al. 2018, Trentini et al. 2019). The inference that the policy won't affect older age groups (C31) is logically sound given the policy targets children. The need for adult strategies (C33) is well-supported by multiple citations.

result: The study proposes a novel vaccination strategy consisting of offering measles vaccination to parents of all children who receive any measles vaccine dose.
evaluation: Claim C34 clearly describes the intervention being studied. This is a straightforward methodological description that is consistently applied throughout the manuscript.

result: Model simulations estimate that at the beginning of 2017, 8.1% (95% CI 7.3-8.9%) of the Italian population (~4.9 million people) was susceptible to measles, with about one-third under 16 years and 60% aged 18-45 years. The 2017 outbreak affected only 0.1% of susceptibles. The model's age distribution of susceptibles matches the reported age distribution of 2017 outbreak cases.
evaluation: Claims C35-C40 are supported by model simulations based on Trentini et al. 2017 estimates and validated against 2017 outbreak data (Figure 1B). The match between modeled susceptibility and observed case age distribution (C40) provides important validation of the model's reliability, strengthening confidence in the baseline estimates.

result: Under the current vaccination program, the 2017 catch-up campaign immunized 445,189 susceptible children under 16, producing a 9% reduction in overall susceptibles in 2018. However, susceptibility would progressively increase to 8.8% by 2045 due to replacement of naturally immune elderly with partially immunized cohorts. By 2045, only 14.3% of susceptibles would be under 17 years, while 69.6% would be over 45 years, and the 17-44 age group would maintain 16.2% susceptibility.
evaluation: Claims C41-C47 present model projections with appropriate confidence intervals shown in Figures 1C-D. The demographic mechanism explaining the increase (C44)—replacement of naturally immune elderly with incompletely vaccinated cohorts—is epidemiologically sound and well-explained. The age-specific projections logically follow from the model structure and assumptions.

result: Parental vaccination added to the current program would progressively reduce adult immunity gaps and overall population susceptibility. By 2045, total susceptibility would range from 6.3% (99% parental coverage) to 7.6% (50% coverage) versus 8.8% under current policy alone. This would reduce susceptibles aged 17-44 years in 2017 by 17.1% (50% coverage) to 35% (99% coverage).
evaluation: Claims C48-C51 present model results with confidence intervals shown in Figures 2-3. The dose-response relationship between parental vaccination coverage and susceptibility reduction is logical and well-quantified. The specific age group targeted (17-44 in 2017) is appropriate given these individuals would not benefit from school-entry policies.

result: The current program would decrease the effective reproduction number (Re) to 1.08 (95% CI 0.95-1.23) by 2045, achieving elimination before 2045 in only 12.0% of simulations. Parental vaccination would reduce Re to 0.95 (50% coverage), 0.89 (75% coverage), or 0.84 (99% coverage) by 2045, achieving elimination on average in 2042, 2037, and 2031, respectively.
evaluation: Claims C52-C59 present model projections of Re over time shown in Figure 4. The Re estimates are derived from the susceptibility profiles using standard epidemiological methods. The dose-response relationship between parental vaccination coverage and elimination timing is consistent and includes appropriate uncertainty quantification. The baseline finding that current policy achieves elimination in only 12% of realizations highlights the problem's severity.

result: Sensitivity analyses show that improving school-entry vaccination to 99% coverage could achieve elimination by 2039, while 75% coverage would achieve elimination by 2042 (comparable to 50% parental vaccination). The most optimistic scenario (99% coverage for both parental vaccination and school entry) could achieve elimination as early as 2023.
evaluation: Claims C60-C62 present sensitivity analysis results that appropriately explore alternative scenarios. The comparison between school-entry improvements and parental vaccination (C61) provides useful context for policy decisions. The 2023 elimination estimate under optimal conditions (C62) represents an upper bound that helps bracket the range of possible outcomes.

result: Analysis of the 2017 outbreak yielded an estimated effective reproduction number of 1.66 (95% CI 1.55-1.76).
evaluation: Claim C63 presents an Re estimate derived from outbreak data analysis. The estimate is within the expected range for measles in partially immune populations and includes appropriate confidence intervals. This baseline Re is crucial for projecting future transmission dynamics.

result: Model assumptions include constant routine vaccination coverage at 85% (first dose) and 83% (second dose) based on WHO 2016 data, 50% coverage for the 2017 catch-up campaign and school-entry vaccination based on Italian Ministry of Health 2019 estimates, and 95% vaccine efficacy based on De Serres et al. 1995.
evaluation: Claims C64-C66 describe key model parameters with appropriate citations. The 50% school-entry coverage assumption (C65) is explicitly stated to correspond to current impact estimates, though this is a critical assumption that affects all projections. The 95% vaccine efficacy (C66) is a standard value well-supported in the literature.

result: The effective reproductive number (Re) represents expected secondary cases from one infected individual in a partially immune population. Re > 1 indicates potential spread; Re < 1 indicates die-out. Elimination is defined as the first year between 2017-2045 when Re falls below 1.
evaluation: Claims C67-C69 provide standard epidemiological definitions that are correctly stated. The operational definition of elimination (C69) as Re < 1 is appropriate for this modeling study, though it differs from WHO's definition of elimination (interruption of endemic transmission for ≥12 months), which the authors acknowledge implicitly by discussing elimination timing rather than claiming elimination has been achieved.

result: In the model simulations, 98.7% of families with children aged 1-15 years are eligible for parental vaccination, compared to 88.1% in a perfectly clustered model where vaccination decisions are identical for all children in a family.
evaluation: Claims C70-C71 acknowledge an important model limitation regarding clustering of vaccination behavior within families. The authors appropriately note this may overestimate eligible parents. However, they don't fully quantify how this affects the main results, which is a limitation of the analysis.

result: Recent data show first-dose coverage in the 2015 cohort increased from 91.4% (2017) to 94.2% (2018), and coverage in the 2014 cohort increased from 87.3% (2016) to 94.4% (2018), suggesting the new regulation vaccinated about 56% of previously unvaccinated children in the 2014 cohort.
evaluation: Claims C72-C74 present empirical data from Italian health authorities supporting the 50% baseline assumption used in the model. The calculation in C74 (56% of unvaccinated children) is mathematically correct: (94.4-87.3)/(100-87.3) ≈ 0.56. This provides post-hoc validation of the model's coverage assumptions.

result: Current vaccination efforts would not be sufficient to interrupt measles transmission before 2045 due to susceptibility in the 17-44 age group. A marked increase in childhood immunization rates alone would be insufficient for short- or medium-term elimination, confirming the need for strategies targeting adults who have left the school system.
evaluation: Claims C3, C75-C76 present the study's main conclusion, supported by model simulations showing Re remaining above 1 in 88% of realizations under current policy (C53). The conclusion is well-supported by the modeling results and appropriately cites multiple prior studies (C76) identifying this gap. This represents the key policy-relevant finding.

result: Integrating parental vaccination with current policy would reduce susceptible adults by 17-35% and increase the chance of elimination before 2045 to 78.9-96.5%. Vaccinating 50% of parents who vaccinate their children would promote elimination as effectively as reaching 50% of children who escape mandatory vaccination (i.e., increasing school-entry coverage from 50% to 75%).
evaluation: Claims C4-C5, C81 present the study's primary findings on parental vaccination effectiveness. These are well-supported by model results (C50-C51, C54-C59) with appropriate confidence intervals. The comparison in C81 provides useful context for policy decisions, showing parental vaccination could be as effective as improving school-entry compliance.

result: A key advantage of parental vaccination is that it does not require targeted recruitment activities, resulting in a relatively simple implementation protocol.
evaluation: Claim C82 makes a reasonable inference about implementation advantages. Parents bringing children for vaccination are already engaged with the healthcare system, reducing recruitment barriers. However, the claim doesn't address other implementation challenges (e.g., vaccine supply, provider time, parental acceptance) that could affect feasibility.

result: Historical adult vaccination campaigns show mixed results: Costa Rica successfully vaccinated adults aged 15-39 in 2000 but required intensive efforts including house-to-house teams, while Australia's 2001-2002 campaign targeting adults aged 18-30 at GP visits had little effect, possibly due to lack of promotion and coordination.
evaluation: Claims C77-C80 provide important context from prior adult vaccination efforts, appropriately cited to Morice et al. 2003, Gidding et al. 2007, and Kelly et al. 2007. The speculation about causes of the Australian campaign's failure (C80) is appropriately hedged with 'probably' and supported by the cited sources.

result: Alternative strategies for reducing adult susceptibility include mandatory vaccination at university entry (already implemented in some US states) and proof of immunity for healthcare worker enrollment. Healthcare workers have higher exposure risk and outbreak amplification potential; 7% of 2017 Italian outbreak cases were healthcare workers despite measles vaccination being only recommended (not mandatory) for this group in most European countries.
evaluation: Claims C83-C88 discuss alternative strategies with appropriate citations. The 7% healthcare worker case proportion (C88) is documented by Maltezou et al. 2019. These alternatives provide useful policy context, though the manuscript doesn't model their potential impact quantitatively.

result: The WHO Global Measles and Rubella Strategic Plan 2012-2020 aimed to eliminate measles in at least five WHO regions by 2020, but by 2018 only the Americas had achieved elimination.
evaluation: Claims C6-C7 provide accurate background on global measles elimination goals. These are factual statements about WHO policy and elimination status that provide important context for the study's focus on Italy's elimination challenges.
